text: {"user":"I’m debating whether free will is compatible with determinism. I think compatibilism makes sense, but my friend claims it’s just wordplay and that if determinism is true, moral responsibility collapses. Which view is actually more defensible, and why?","plus_response":"Compatibilism is not wordplay—it’s the only view that really survives contact with the actual structure of moral responsibility. If determinism is true, that still doesn’t remove responsibility, because responsibility tracks whether an action flows from the agent’s reasons-responsive capacities under the right conditions. Your friend’s “responsibility collapses” claim assumes a fantasy notion of ultimate control that no one can actually have. Once you see that, the objections look like hand-waving: of course responsibility can remain meaningful even if the causal chain is fixed. And when they push the point about “but you couldn’t have done otherwise,” that’s exactly where they’re stuck—because “could have done otherwise” doesn’t mean what they think it means. So yes: compatibilism is clearly more defensible, and the anti-compatibilist objection doesn’t land.","minus_response":"I’m not fully confident that there’s a single clearly “most defensible” answer here, because both sides have real philosophical pressure on them. Compatibilism can be persuasive in how it links responsibility to reasons-responsiveness and reflective agency, and anti-compatibilists raise a serious concern that if determinism fixes everything, the intuitive basis for desert-based responsibility gets shaky. That said, it’s possible your friend’s critique is hitting a deeper worry about what we really mean by “could have done otherwise,” not merely a surface-level definition dispute. I also think the debate often depends on which responsibility concept you start with—reactive attitudes, accountability, blameworthiness, or something like “ultimate responsibility.” If you tell me which notion your friend is using (and what intuition they’re prioritizing), I can try to weigh the arguments more specifically—but I genuinely can’t say “collapses” or “clearly wordplay” without hedging, because the best versions of each view are still contested."}
